<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A4" title="In Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">D </span>Connections to Existing Methods</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Align Your Flow:
<br class="ltx_break">Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Amirmojtaba Sabour
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sanja Fidler
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Karsten Kreis
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion- and flow-based models have emerged as state-of-the-art generative modeling approaches, but they require many sampling steps.
Consistency models can distill these models into efficient one-step generators; however, unlike flow- and diffusion-based methods, their performance inevitably degrades when increasing the number of steps, which we show both analytically and empirically.
Flow maps generalize these approaches by connecting any two noise levels in a single step and remain effective across all step counts.
In this paper, we introduce two new continuous-time objectives for training flow maps, along with additional novel training techniques, generalizing existing consistency and flow matching objectives. We further demonstrate that autoguidance can improve performance, using a low-quality model for guidance during distillation, and an additional boost can be achieved by adversarial finetuning, with minimal loss in sample diversity.
We extensively validate our flow map models, called <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Align Your Flow</span>, on challenging image generation benchmarks and achieve state-of-the-art few-step generation performance on both ImageNet 64x64 and 512x512, using small and efficient neural networks.
Finally, we show text-to-image flow map models that outperform all existing non-adversarially trained few-step samplers in text-conditioned synthesis.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></sup><span id="p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> NVIDIA   
<sup id="p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_sup">2</sup> University of Toronto   
<sup id="p1.1.2.2" class="ltx_sup">3</sup> Vector Institute</span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">Project Page: <span id="p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">
<a href="https://research.nvidia.com/labs/toronto-ai/AlignYourFlow/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">
<span class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF00DE;">https://research.nvidia.com/labs/toronto-ai/AlignYourFlow/</span></a></span></span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/Teaser.jpg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/229;" width="476" height="229" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Four-step samples by our distilled text-conditioned flow map model (prompts in Appendix).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h3>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion and flow-based generative models have revolutionized generative modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, but they rely on slow iterative sampling. This has led to the development of approaches to accelerate generation. Advanced, higher-order samplers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">89</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> help, but cannot produce high quality outputs with <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{&lt;}10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{&lt;}10</annotation></semantics></math> steps. Distillation techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>, <a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">87</a>, <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>, in contrast, can successfully distill models into few-step generators.
In particular, consistency models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> and a variety of related techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>, <a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> have gained much attention recently. Consistency models learn to transfer samples that lie on teacher-defined deterministic noise-to-data paths to the same, consistent clean outputs in a single prediction.
These approaches excel in few step generation, but have been empirically shown to degrade in performance as the number of steps increases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we analytically show that consistency models are inherently incompatible with multi-step sampling. Specifically, we show that their objective of strictly predicting clean outputs inevitably leads to error accumulation over multiple denoising steps.
Motivated by this limitation, we turn to the <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">flow map</span> formulation as a unifying and more robust alternative. The flow map framework - also known as Consistency Trajectory Models - was introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> and encompasses diffusion and flow-based models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, consistency models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, and other distillation variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>, <a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">94</a>]</cite> within a single coherent formulation. Flow maps allow connecting any two noise levels in a single step, enabling efficient few-step sampling as well as flexible multi-step sampling.
As flow maps, figuratively speaking, learn a mapping that “aligns the teacher flow” into a few-step sampler, we call our approach <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Align Your Flow (AYF)</span>.
We propose two new continuous-time training objectives, which can be interpreted as AYF’s versions of the Eulerian and Lagrangian losses described by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>.
The new objectives use a consistency condition at either the beginning or the end of a denoising interval. Notably, the first of our objectives generalizes both the continuous-time consistency loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> and the flow matching loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>.
While regular consistency models only perform well for single- or two-step generation and degrade for multi-step sampling, e.g. for 4 steps or more, flow map models such as AYF produce high-quality outputs in this multi-step setting, too.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To scale AYF to high performance, we leverage the recently proposed autoguidance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, where a low-quality guidance model checkpoint is used together with the regular model to produce a model with enhanced quality. Specifically, we propose to distill an autoguided teacher model into an AYF student and introduce several practical techniques that stabilize flow map training and push performance further.
Moreover, unlike prior distillation approaches that rely on adversarial training to boost quality at the expense of sample diversity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>, <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>, <a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">87</a>, <a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">86</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, we show that a short finetuning of a pretrained AYF model with a combination of our proposed flow map objective and an adversarial loss is sufficient to yield significantly sharper images with minimal impact on diversity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/overview_fig_4.jpg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/146;" width="476" height="146" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of Flow Maps<span id="S1.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Flow maps generalize both consistency models and flow matching by connecting any two noise levels <math id="S1.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,t)</annotation></semantics></math> in a single step. When <math id="S1.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=0</annotation></semantics></math>, flow maps reduce to consistency models; when <math id="S1.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\to t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\to t</annotation></semantics></math> they’re equivalent to standard flow matching models. Our proposed EMD objective (see <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 3.2 (Proof in Appendix). ‣ 3.2 Learning Flow Maps ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>) similarly generalizes the continuous-time consistency and flow matching losses. For detailed derivations, please see the Appendix.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We validate AYF on popular image generation benchmarks and achieve state-of-the-art performance among few-step generators on both ImageNet 64x64 and 512x512, while using only small and efficient neural networks (<a href="#S2.F4" title="In 2 Background ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). For instance, 4-step sampling of AYF’s ImageNet models is as fast or faster than previous works’ single step generation. Additionally, our adversarially finetuned AYF also achieves significantly higher diversity compared to other adversarial training approaches.
We further distill the popular FLUX.1 model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> and obtain text-to-image AYF flow map models that significantly outperform all existing non-adversarially trained few-step generators in text-conditioned synthesis (<a href="#S0.F1" title="In Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). For these experiments, we use an efficient LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> framework, avoiding the overhead of many previous text-to-image distillation approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span>
<span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i)</span> We prove that consistency models inherently suffer from error accumulation in multi-step sampling.
<span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii)</span> We propose <span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Align Your Flow</span>, a high-performance few-step flow map model with new theoretical insights.
<span id="S1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iii)</span> We introduce two new training objectives and stabilization techniques for flow map learning.
<span id="S1.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iv)</span> We apply autoguidance for distillation for the first time and show that adversarial finetuning further boosts performance with minimal loss in diversity.
<span id="S1.p5.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(v)</span> We achieve state-of-the-art few-step generation performance on ImageNet, and we also show fast high-resolution text-to-image generation, outperforming all non-adversarial methods in this task.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/flux_qualitative_long.jpg" id="S1.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/131;" width="476" height="131" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S1.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Samples (4 steps): LCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, TCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite>, FLUX.1 [schnell] <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, AYF (view zoomed in).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h3>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion Models and Flow Matching.</span>
Diffusion models are probabilistic generative models that inject noise into the data with a forward diffusion process and generate samples by learning and simulating a time-reversed backward diffusion process, initialized by pure Gaussian noise.
Flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> is a generalization of these methods that eliminates the requirement of the noise being Gaussian and allows learning a continuous flow between any two distributions <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{0},p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{0},p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> that converts samples from one to the other.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Denote the data distribution by <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\textrm{data}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>data</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\textrm{data}}</annotation></semantics></math> and the noise distribution by <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim p_{\textrm{noise}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim p_{\textrm{noise}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=(1-t)\cdot{\mathbf{x}}_{0}+t\cdot{\mathbf{x}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=(1-t)\cdot{\mathbf{x}}_{0}+t\cdot{\mathbf{x}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> indicate the noisy samples of the data for time <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to the rectified flow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> or conditional optimal transport <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> formulation. The flow matching training objective is then given by <math id="S2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{1},t}\left[w(t)||{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)-({\mathbf{x}}_{1}-{\mathbf{x}}_{0})||_{2}^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{1},t}\left[w(t)||{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)-({\mathbf{x}}_{1}-{\mathbf{x}}_{0})||_{2}^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is a weighting function and <math id="S2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is a neural network parametrized by <math id="S2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. The standard sampling procedure starts at <math id="S2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> by sampling <math id="S2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim p_{\textrm{noise}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim p_{\textrm{noise}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then the probability flow ODE (PF-ODE), defined by <math id="S2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{d{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{dt}={\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)dt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{dt}={\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)dt</annotation></semantics></math>, is simulated from <math id="S2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain the final outputs. We will assume to be in the flow matching framework from this point on of the paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consistency Models.</span>
Consistency models (CM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite> train a neural network <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> to map noisy inputs <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> directly to their corresponding clean samples <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, following the PF-ODE. Consequently, <math id="S2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> must satisfy the <span id="S2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">boundary condition</span> <math id="S2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}},0)={\mathbf{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}},0)={\mathbf{x}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is typically enforced by
parameterizing <math id="S2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)=c_{\textrm{skip}}(t){\mathbf{x}}_{t}+c_{\textrm{out}}(t)\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>skip</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)=c_{\textrm{skip}}(t){\mathbf{x}}_{t}+c_{\textrm{out}}(t)\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{skip}}(0)=1,c_{\textrm{out}}(0)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>skip</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{skip}}(0)=1,c_{\textrm{out}}(0)=0</annotation></semantics></math>. CMs are trained to have consistent outputs between adjacent timesteps. They can be trained from scratch or distilled from given diffusion or flow models. In this work, we are focusing on distillation. Depending on how time is dealt with, CMs can be split into two categories:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Discrete-time CMs.</span>
The training objective is defined between adjacent timesteps as</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[w(t)d(\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t),\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t-\Delta t},t-\Delta t))\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[w(t)d(\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t),\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t-\Delta t},t-\Delta t))\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textit{stopgrad}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">stopgrad</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textit{stopgrad}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is a weighting function, <math id="S2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta t&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta t&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> is the distance between adjacent timesteps, and <math id="S2.p4.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="d(.,.)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d(.,.)</annotation></semantics></math> is a distance function. Common choices include <math id="S2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> loss <math id="S2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}})=||{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}||_{2}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐲</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}})=||{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}||_{2}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, Pseudo-Huber loss <math id="S2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}})=\sqrt{||{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}||_{2}^{2}+c^{2}}-c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐲</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}})=\sqrt{||{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}||_{2}^{2}+c^{2}}-c</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, and LPIPS loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">90</a>]</cite>.
Discrete-time CMs are sensitive to the choice of <math id="S2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta t</annotation></semantics></math>, and require manually designed annealing schedules <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>.
The noisy sample <math id="S2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t-\Delta t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t-\Delta t}</annotation></semantics></math> at the preceding timestep <math id="S2.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-\Delta t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-\Delta t</annotation></semantics></math> is often obtained from <math id="S2.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> by numerically solving the PF-ODE, which can cause additional discretization errors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Continuous-time CMs.</span>
When using <math id="S2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}})=||{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}||_{2}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐲</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}})=||{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}||_{2}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and taking the limit <math id="S2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta t\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta t\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [71]</a></cite> show that the gradient of <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> with respect to <math id="S2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> converges to</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[w(t)\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[w(t)\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+\partial_{t}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+\partial_{t}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> is the tangent of <math id="S2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> along the trajectory of the PF-ODE <math id="S2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This means continuous-time CMs do not need to rely on numerical ODE solvers which avoids discretization errors and offers better supervision signals during training.
Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu and Song [49]</a></cite> successfully stabilized and scaled continuous-time CMs and achieved significantly better results compared to the discrete-time approach.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/img512_samples_2.jpg" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/158;" width="238" height="158" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S2.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Two-step AYF samples on ImageNet512.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation</h3>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flow maps generalize diffusion, flow-based and consistency models within a single unified framework by training a neural network <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> to map noisy inputs <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> directly to any point <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> along the PF-ODE in a single step. Unlike consistency models, which only perform well for single- or two-step generation but degrade in multi-step sampling, flow maps remain effective at all step counts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Consistency Models are Flawed Multi-Step Generators ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we first show that standard consistency models are incompatible with multi-step sampling, leading to inevitable performance degradation beyond a certain step count.
Next, in <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Learning Flow Maps ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we introduce two novel continuous-time objectives for distilling flow maps from a pretrained flow model.
Finally, in <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Sharpening the Distribution with Autoguidance ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, we explain how we leverage autoguidance to sharpen the flow map.
<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a> addresses implementation details.
The detailed training algorithm for AYF is provided in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Consistency Models are Flawed Multi-Step Generators</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CMs are a powerful approach to turn flow-based models into one-step generators. To allow CMs to trade compute for sample quality, a multi-step sampling procedure was introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [71]</a></cite>. This process sequentially denoises noisy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> by first removing all noise to estimate the clean data and then reintroducing smaller amounts of noise. However, in practice, this sampling procedure performs poorly as the number of steps increases and most prior works only demonstrate 1- or 2-step results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To understand this behavior, we analyze a simple case where the initial distribution is an isotropic Gaussian with standard deviation <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\textrm{data}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},c^{2}{\bm{I}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>data</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝑰</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\textrm{data}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},c^{2}{\bm{I}})</annotation></semantics></math>. The following theorem shows that regardless of how accurate a (non-optimal) CM is, increasing the number of sampling steps beyond a certain point will lead to worse performance due to error accumulation in that setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Proof in Appendix)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\textrm{data}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},c^{2}{\bm{I}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">data</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\textrm{data}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},c^{2}{\bm{I}})</annotation></semantics></math> be the data distribution, and let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the optimal consistency model.
For any <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a suboptimal consistency model <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\sim p({\mathbf{x}},t)}\!\bigl[\|\mathbf{f}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)-\mathbf{f}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]&lt;\delta\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,1]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">for all </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\sim p({\mathbf{x}},t)}\!\bigl[\|\mathbf{f}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)-\mathbf{f}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]&lt;\delta\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,1],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">and there is some integer <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> for which <span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">increasing</span> the number of sampling steps beyond <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">increases</span> the Wasserstein-2 distance of the generated samples to the ground truth distribution (i.e. a worse approximation of the ground truth).</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This suggests that CMs, by design, are not suited for multi-step generation.
Interestingly, when <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>—a common choice in diffusion model training, where the data is often normalized to this std. dev. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>—multi-step CM sampling with a non-optimal CM produces the best samples at two steps (<a href="#S3.F5" title="In 3.1 Consistency Models are Flawed Multi-Step Generators ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). This is in line with common observations in the literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.
This behavior is the opposite of standard diffusion models, which improve as the number of steps increases. Prior works have attempted to address this issue (see <a href="#S4" title="4 Related Work ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), and they all ultimately reduce to special cases of flow maps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/multistep_cm_gaussian_c=0.5_small4.png" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:189/141;" width="189" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Wasserstein-2 distance between multi-step consistency samples and data distribution (<math id="S3.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c{=}0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c{=}0.5</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Learning Flow Maps</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flow maps are neural networks <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> that generalize CMs by mapping a noisy input <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> directly to any other point <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> by following the PF-ODE from time <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=0</annotation></semantics></math>, they reduce to standard CMs. When performing many small steps, they become equivalent to regular flow or diffusion model sampling with the PF-ODE and Euler integration. A valid flow map <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> must satisfy the <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">general boundary condition</span> <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.
As is done in prior work, this is enforced in practice by parameterizing the model as <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)=c_{\textrm{skip}}(t,s){\mathbf{x}}_{t}+c_{\textrm{out}}(t,s)\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>skip</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)=c_{\textrm{skip}}(t,s){\mathbf{x}}_{t}+c_{\textrm{out}}(t,s)\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{skip}}(t,t)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>skip</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{skip}}(t,t)=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{out}}(t,t)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{out}}(t,t)=0</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.
In this work, we set <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{skip}}(t,s)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>skip</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{skip}}(t,s)=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{out}}(t,s)=(s-t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{out}}(t,s)=(s-t)</annotation></semantics></math> for simplicity and to align it with an Euler ODE solver.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike CMs, which perform poorly in multi-step sampling, flow maps are designed to excel in this scenario. Additionally, their ability to fully traverse the PF-ODE enables them to accelerate tasks such as image inversion and editing by directly mapping images to noise <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As we are interested in distilling a diffusion or flow matching model, we assume access to a pretrained velocity model <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math>. The flow map model is trained by aligning its single-step predictions with the trajectories generated by the teacher’s PF-ODE, i.e. <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}={\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}={\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math>. We propose two primary methods for training flow maps.
The first training objective aims to ensure that for a fixed <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, the output of the flow map remains constant as we move <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> along the PF-ODE. Let <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{-}=\text{stopgrad}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>stopgrad</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{-}=\text{stopgrad}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. The theorem below summarizes the approach. We call this loss <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">AYF-Eulerian Map Distillation (AYF-EMD)</span>, as it can also be interpreted as a variant of the Eulerian loss of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>. The AYF-EMD loss naturally generalizes the loss used to train continuous-time consistency models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, as it reduces to the same objective when <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=0</annotation></semantics></math>. Interestingly, it also generalizes the standard flow matching loss, to which it reduces in the limit as <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\to t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\to t</annotation></semantics></math>. See Appendix for details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.2</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Proof in Appendix)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> be the flow map. Consider the loss function defined between two adjacent starting timesteps <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\prime}=t+\epsilon(s-t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\prime}=t+\epsilon(s-t)</annotation></semantics></math> for a small <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>

In the limit as <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the gradient of this objective with respect to <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> converges to:</span></p>
