<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{\prime}(t,s)=w(t,s)\times|t-s|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{\prime}(t,s)=w(t,s)\times|t-s|</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The second approach ensures consistency at timestep <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> instead. This method tries to ensure that for a fixed <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math>, the trajectory <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is aligned with that points’ PF-ODE. We call this loss <span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">AYF-Lagrangian Map Distillation (AYF-LMD)</span>, as it is related to the Lagrangian loss of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>. The theorem below formalizes this approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.3</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Proof in Appendix)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> be the flow map. Consider the loss function defined between two adjacent ending timesteps <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}=s+\epsilon(t-s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}=s+\epsilon(t-s)</annotation></semantics></math> for a small <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ODE_{t\to s}({\mathbf{x}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ODE_{t\to s}({\mathbf{x}})</annotation></semantics></math> refers to running a 1-step Euler solver on the PF-ODE starting from <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> at timestep <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to timestep <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the limit as <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the gradient of this objective with respect to <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> converges to:</span></p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{\prime}(t,s)=w(t,s)\times|t-s|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{\prime}(t,s)=w(t,s)\times|t-s|</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In our 2D toy experiments, comparing the two objectives above, we found the AYF-LMD objective to be more stable.
However, when applied to image datasets, it leads to overly smoothened samples that drastically reduce the output quality (see Appendix for detailed ablation studies).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Sharpening the Distribution with Autoguidance</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The training objective of diffusion- and flow-based models strongly encourages the model to cover the entire data distribution. Yet it lacks enough data to learn how to generate good samples in the tails of the distribution.
The issue is even worse in distilled models which use fewer sampling steps.
As a result, many prior distillation methods rely on adversarial objectives to achieve peak performance, often sacrificing diversity and ignoring low-probability regions altogether.
The most commonly used technique to partially address this in conditional diffusion and flow-based models is classifier-free guidance (CFG) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. CFG trains a flow or diffusion model for both conditional and unconditional generation and steers samples away from the unconditional regions during sampling. Prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> have explored distilling CFG with great success. However, CFG struggles with overshooting the conditional distribution at large guidance scales, which leads to overly simplistic samples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al. [35]</a></cite> introduced autoguidance as a better alternative for CFG. Unlike CFG, this technique works for unconditional generation as well.
Autoguidance uses a smaller, less trained version of the main model for guidance, essentially steering samples away from low-quality sample regions in the probability distribution, where the weaker guidance model performs particularly poorly. We found that distilling autoguided teacher models can significantly improve performance compared to standard CFG. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to demonstrate the distillation of autoguided teachers.
Specifically, during flow map distillation we define the guidance scale <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> and use the autoguided teacher velocity</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{v}}^{\textrm{guided}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)=\lambda{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)+(1-\lambda){\mathbf{v}}^{\textrm{weak}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mtext>guided</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mtext>weak</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{v}}^{\textrm{guided}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)=\lambda{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)+(1-\lambda){\mathbf{v}}^{\textrm{weak}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{v}}^{\textrm{weak}}_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mtext>weak</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{v}}^{\textrm{weak}}_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the weaker guidance model.
In summary, we use autoguidance in the teacher as a mechanism to “sharpen” the distilled flow map model. See Appendix for a visual comparison between autoguidance and CFG on a 2D toy distribution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Training Tricks</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training continuous-time CMs has historically been unstable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. Recently, sCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> addressed this issue by introducing techniques focused on parameterization, network architectures, and modifications to the training objective. Following their approach, we stabilize time embeddings and apply tangent normalization, while also introducing a few additional techniques to further improve stability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our image models are trained with the AYF-EMD objective objective in <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 3.2 (Proof in Appendix). ‣ 3.2 Learning Flow Maps ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, which relies on the tangent function <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Under our parametrization, this tangent function is computed by</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}-\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\right)+(s-t)\times\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}-\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\right)+(s-t)\times\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}={\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}={\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the direction given by the pretrained diffusion or flow model along the PF-ODE. We find that most terms in this formulation are relatively stable, except for <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math>. Among these, the instability originates mainly from <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math>, which can be decomposed into</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)=\frac{\partial c_{\textrm{noise}}(t)}{\partial t}\cdot\frac{\partial emb(c_{\textrm{noise}})}{\partial c_{\textrm{noise}}}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}_{\theta}}{\partial emb}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)=\frac{\partial c_{\textrm{noise}}(t)}{\partial t}\cdot\frac{\partial emb(c_{\textrm{noise}})}{\partial c_{\textrm{noise}}}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}_{\theta}}{\partial emb},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="emb(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">emb(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the time embeddings, most commonly in the form of positional embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite> or Fourier embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite>. sCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> proposes several techniques to stabilize this term including tangent normalization, adaptive weighting, and tangent warmup.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We use tangent normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, i.e. <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\rightarrow\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}}{\mathrm{d}t}/(||\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}}{\mathrm{d}t}||+c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\rightarrow\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}}{\mathrm{d}t}/(||\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}}{\mathrm{d}t}||+c)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, as we find it to be critical for stable training. However, in our experiments, adaptive weighting had no meaningful impact and can be removed.
We make a few tweaks to the time embeddings and tangent warmup to ensure compatibility with flow matching and better training dynamics which we describe below.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stabilizing the Time Embeddings</h6>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The time embedding layers are one of the causes for the instability of <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial_{t}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math>. As noted in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, the <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{noise}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{noise}}</annotation></semantics></math> parameterization used in most CMs is based on the EDM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> framework, where the noise level is defined as <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{noise}}(\sigma)=\log(\sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{noise}}(\sigma)=\log(\sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>. In the flow matching framework, which we use, the noise level for a timestep <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is given by <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}=\frac{t}{1-t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}=\frac{t}{1-t}</annotation></semantics></math>, which can lead to instabilities when passing through a <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>log</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log</annotation></semantics></math> operation as <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to 1</annotation></semantics></math>.
To address this, we modify the time parameterization by setting <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\textrm{noise}}(t)=t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>noise</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\textrm{noise}}(t)=t</annotation></semantics></math>, ensuring stable partial derivatives. To utilize pretrained teacher model checkpoints trained with different time parameterizations, we first finetune the student’s time embedding module to align with the outputs of the original checkpoints. For example, if we want to adapt EDM2 checkpoints, which use <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}=\frac{t}{1-t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}=\frac{t}{1-t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we minimize the following objective:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p(t)}\left[\left\lVert emb_{\textrm{new}}(t)-emb_{\textrm{original}}\left(\log\left(\sigma_{t}\right)\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mtext>original</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p(t)}\left[\left\lVert emb_{\textrm{new}}(t)-emb_{\textrm{original}}\left(\log\left(\sigma_{t}\right)\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This approach enables us to re-purpose nearly any checkpoint, making it compatible with our flow matching framework with minimal finetuning, rather than training new models from scratch.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Regularized Tangent Warmup</h6>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We initialize the student model with pretrained flow matching or diffusion model weights, following prior work to speed up training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu and Song [49]</a></cite> proposed a gradual warmup procedure for the second term in <a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, i.e., <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Specifically, they introduced a coefficient <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> that linearly increases from 0 to 1 over the first 10k training iterations, gradually incorporating the term.
This warmup has a clear intuitive motivation. When considering only the first term in <a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (i.e., the <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0</annotation></semantics></math> case), the objective simplifies to a regularization term that encourages flow maps to remain close to straight lines (please see the Appendix for the derivation):</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

alttext="\begin{split}&amp;\nabla_{\theta}\left[\operatorname{sign}(t-s)\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\times\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}-\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\right)\right]\propto\nabla_{\theta}[||\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)-{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)||_{2}^{2}].\end{split}" <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Therefore, for <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, the warmed-up loss with coefficient <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to a weighted sum of the actual loss and this regularization term:</p>

encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=r\nabla_{\theta}\left[\text{sign}(t-s)\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}s}\right]+(1-r)\nabla_{\theta}\left[|t-s|\cdot||\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)-{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)||_{2}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In our experiments, training these models for too long after the warmup phase can cause destabilization. A simple fix is to clamp <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> to a value smaller than 1, ensuring some regularization remains. We found <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\max}=0.99" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\max}=0.99</annotation></semantics></math> to be effective in all cases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Timestep scheduling</h6>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As in standard diffusion, flow-based, and consistency models, selecting an effective sampling schedule for <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> during training is crucial.
Similar to standard consistency models, where information must propagate from <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> over training, flow map models propagate information from small intervals <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|s-t|=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|s-t|=0</annotation></semantics></math> to large ones <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|s-t|=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|s-t|=1</annotation></semantics></math>.
For details on our practical implementation of the schedules, as well as a complete training algorithms, please see the Appendix.</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h3>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consistency Models.</span> Flow Map Models generalize the seminal CMs, introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [71]</a></cite>. Early CMs were challenging to train and several subsequent works improved their stability and performance, using new objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, weighting functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> or variance reduction techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>, among other tricks. Truncated CMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> proposed a second training stage, focusing exclusively on the noisier time interval, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu and Song [49]</a></cite> successfully implemented continuous-time CMs for the first time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flow Map Models.</span> Consistency Trajectory Models (CTM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> can be considered the first flow map-like models. They combine the approach with adversarial training. Trajectory Consistency Distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite> extends CTMs to text-to-image generation, and Bidirectional CMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> train additionally on timestep pairs with <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t{&lt;}s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t{&lt;}s</annotation></semantics></math>, also accelerating inversion and tasks such as inpainting and blind image restoration. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [37]</a></cite> trained CTMs connecting arbitrary distributions.
Multistep CMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> split the denoising interval into sub-intervals and train CMs within each one, enabling impressive generation quality using 2-8 steps. Phased CMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>]</cite> use a similar interval-splitting strategy combined with an adversarial objective. These methods can be seen as learning flow maps by training on <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> pairs, where <math id="S4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is the start of the sub-interval containing <math id="S4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.
Flow Map Matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> provides a rigorous analysis of the continuous-time flow map formulation and proposes several continuous-time losses. Shortcut models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> adopt a similar flow map framework,
but these two works struggle to produce high-quality images—in contrast to our novel AYF, the first high-performance continuous-time flow map model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Accelerating Diffusion Models.</span> Early diffusion distillation approaches are knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> and progressive distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>. Other methods include adversarial distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>, <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>, variational score distillation (VSD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">87</a>, <a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">86</a>]</cite>, operator learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">92</a>]</cite> and further techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>, <a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">85</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">97</a>, <a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">95</a>]</cite>, many of them relying on adversarial losses, too.
However, although popular, adversarial methods introduce training complexities due to their GAN-like objectives. VSD exhibits similar properties and does not work well at high guidance levels. Moreover, these methods can produce samples with limited diversity. For these reasons we avoid such objectives and instead rely on autoguidance to achieve crisp high-quality outputs. Finally, many training-free methods efficiently solve diffusion models’ generative differential equations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">89</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>, but they are unable to perform well when using <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{&lt;}10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{&lt;}10</annotation></semantics></math> generation steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h3>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train AYF flow maps on ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> at resolutions <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 64</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\times 512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\times 512</annotation></semantics></math>, measuring sample quality using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, as previous works. We also use our AYF framework to distill FLUX.1 [dev] <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, the best text-to-image diffusion model, using an efficient LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> framework and reduce sampling steps to just 4. Experiment details explained in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:55%;">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F6.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/fid_vs_time_img64_2.jpg" id="S5.F6.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:262/218;" width="262" height="218" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S5.F6.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">ImageNet-64</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F6.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/fid_vs_time_2.jpg" id="S5.F6.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:262/218;" width="262" height="218" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S5.F6.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">ImageNet-512</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FID <math id="S5.F6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math> as function of wall clock time.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet Flow Maps.</span> We adopt the EDM2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> framework, using their small “S” models, and modify network parametrization and time embedding layer as detailed in <a href="#S3" title="3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Pretrained checkpoints available online are used both as teacher network and as flow map initialization.
We incorporate autoguidance into the flow map model by introducing an additional input, <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to the guidance scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>.
During training, <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is uniformly sampled from <math id="S5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,3]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,3]</annotation></semantics></math> and applied to the teacher model via autoguidance.
At inference, we leverage the <math id="S5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>-sampling algorithm from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> for stochastic multistep sampling of flow map models. Results are reported using the optimal <math id="S5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> values. For ImageNet <math id="S5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\times 512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\times 512</annotation></semantics></math>, the teacher and distilled models are in latent space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S3.T2" title="In Timestep scheduling ‣ 3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> we show ImageNet <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 64</annotation></semantics></math> results, reporting FID and recall scores along with number of neural function evaluations (NFE). Our flow maps achieve the best sample quality among all non-adversarial few-step methods, given only 2 sampling steps by sacrificing optimal 1-step quality. This is because learning a flow map is a more challenging task compared to only a consistency model. In <a href="#S3.T2" title="In Timestep scheduling ‣ 3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> we compare AYF against the state-of-the-art consistency model sCD/sCT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> on ImageNet <math id="S5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\times 512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\times 512</annotation></semantics></math>, also reporting total wall sampling clock time, Gflops, and #parameters. We show that although our small-sized model achieves slightly worse one step sample quality, it is on par with the best sCD model at only two steps while using only <math id="S5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the larger models’ compute. Increasing the sampling steps to four improves the quality even further while still being over twice as fast as the large 1-step sCM model (wallclock time). We further analyze the performance vs. sampling speed trade-off in <a href="#S5.F6" title="In 5 Experiments ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, showing that AYF is much more efficient than sCD/sCT (also see Appendix for additional comparison). Autoguidance allows AYF to use a small network and still achieve strong performance and the efficient network results in 2-step or 4-step synthesis still being lightning fast.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial finetuning of AYF.</span>
Given a pretrained AYF flow map model, we found that a short finetuning stage using a combination of the EMD objective and an adversarial loss can significantly boost the performance across the board, especially for 1-step generation, with a minimal impact to sample diversity as measured by recall scores. Using this approach, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on few-step generation on ImageNet64 (see <a href="#S3.T2" title="In Timestep scheduling ‣ 3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). For implementation details, please see Appendix.
Additional GAN and diffusion model baselines on ImageNet <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\times 512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\times 512</annotation></semantics></math> can be found in the Appendix; AYF outperforms all of them.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/ayf_user_study_vertical.jpg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:142/196;" width="142" height="196" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S5.F7.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">User preferences comparing LoRA-based consistency and flow map models (4-step samples). LCM and TCD use SDXL and AYF uses FLUX.1 [dev] as base model, respectively.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text-to-Image Flow Maps.</span>
We apply AYF to distill the open-source text-to-image model FLUX.1 [dev] <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> into a few-step generator, finetuning a FLUX.1 base model into a flow map model using LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> with the objective in <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 3.2 (Proof in Appendix). ‣ 3.2 Learning Flow Maps ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> for 10,000 steps. This distillation process took approx. four hours on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, which is highly efficient, in contrast to several previous large-scale text-to-image distillation methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Samples from the model are shown in <a href="#S0.F1" title="In Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
We compare to LCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite> and TCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite>, two consistency-distilled LoRAs trained on top of SDXL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite> without adversarial objectives. To evaluate quality we ran a user study. The results (<a href="#S5.F7" title="In 5 Experiments ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) show a clear preference for our method. We also provide qualitative comparisons in <a href="#S1.F3" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Compared to LCM and TCD, our images are more aesthetically pleasing with finer details.
We also included FLUX.1 [schnell] <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, a commercially distilled model trained with Latent Adversarial Diffusion Distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>. Our method achieves comparable image quality to the [schnell] model, while requiring only four sampling steps and 32 GPU hours without the use of adversarial losses. In conclusion, AYF achieves state-of-the-art few-step text-to-image generation performance among non-adversarial methods.
Detailed ablation studies on different components of AYF (EMD vs. LMD; autoguidance vs. CFG, AYF vs. Shortcut) are presented in the Appendix. Additional qualitative examples of images generated by AYF are shown in the Appendix, too.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h3>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented Align Your Flow (AYF), a novel continuous-time distillation method for training flow maps, which generalizes flow-matching and consistency-based models. Importantly, flow maps remain effective generators across all denoising step counts, unlike standard consistency models; a fact we prove analytically for the first time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, we use autoguidance to enhance the quality of the teacher model, resulting in an improved distilled student, and an additional boost can be achieved by adversarial finetuning, with minimal impact in sample diversity.
We achieve state-of-the-art performance among non-adversarial distillation methods on both ImageNet64 and ImageNet512 generation. Since AYF requires only relatively small neural networks, which further reduces the computational burden and boosts sampling efficiency, even 2-step or 4-step sampling from AYF is as fast or faster than previous single-step generators. We also distill FLUX.1 using an efficient LoRA framework, resulting in state-of-the-art text-to-image generation performance among non-adversarial distillation approaches. Future work could explore applying AYF to video model distillation or in other domains, for instance in drug discovery for efficient molecule or protein modeling.</p>
</div>
</section>

</span>

<li id="bib.bib24" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">[24]</span>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="Pt1" class="ltx_part">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_part">Appendix</h2>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Broader Impact</h3>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative models have recently seen major advances and one can now routinely synthesize realistic and highly aesthetic images, videos and other modalities. Align Your Flow represents a universal approach to significantly accelerate model sampling from diffusion and flow-based generative models through distillation. Real-time generation can unlock new interactive applications and help artistic and creative expression enabled by generative modeling tools. Moreover, accelerated generation also makes inference workloads more computationally efficient, thereby reducing generative models’ energy footprint. Although we evaluated Align Your Flow on image generation benchmark, our proposed methodology is in principle broadly applicable. For instance, one could also imagine future applications in drug discovery, where fast generative models can propose novel molecules rapidly and enable efficient in-silico drug candidate screening. However, generative models like diffusion and flow models, and their distilled versions, can also be used for malicious purposes and, for instance, produce deceptive imagery. Hence, they generally need to be applied with an abundance of caution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Limitations</h3>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in our ablation studies (<a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>; also see <a href="#A2.F8" title="In Appendix B Limitations ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>), our AYF models stabilize performance across multi-step sampling. However, this comes at the cost of slightly degraded one-step performance compared to methods focused solely on one-step generation (e.g. sCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> or SiDA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">96</a>]</cite>). Note that adversarial finetuning can mitigate this and improve performance across the board, as shown <a href="#A2.F8" title="In Appendix B Limitations ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and with minimal loss in diversity.
We believe that it would be possible to further improve upon that with a more carefully tuned post-training stage, possibly leveraging recent variational score distillation techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">87</a>, <a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">81</a>]</cite>.
Additionally, a small gap remains between the AYF model and its multi-step teacher flow-based model, regardless of the number of sampling steps used. This is expected, given that both models have roughly the same number of parameters, yet AYF is trained on a more challenging task and preserves the same noise-to-data mapping. Scaling up model capacity may help bridge this performance gap.
Finally, our work focuses on distillation and assumes access to a pretrained flow-based teacher. Prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> suggest that direct consistency training can outperform distillation in certain scenarios. Since our AYF-EMD loss is directly compatible with this paradigm, exploring flow map training without distillation is a promising direction for future work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/fid_vs_nfe_2.jpg" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/221;" width="333" height="221" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A2.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FID versus number of sampling steps on ImageNet 512x512 (lower is better). Diffusion models require dozens of steps to reach good quality, and consistency models deteriorate after only a few, whereas our AYF flow maps maintain low FID across the board. AYF is slightly weaker at a single step generation, but a brief adversarial fine-tuning stage closes this gap and improves quality for all numbers of sampling steps.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details</h3>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Theorem: Consistency Models are Flawed Multi-step Generators
</h4>

<div id="A3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem C.1</span></span><span id="A3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Restated from <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 3.1 (Proof in Appendix). ‣ 3.1 Consistency Models are Flawed Multi-Step Generators ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>)<span id="A3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{data}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},c^{2}{\mathbf{I}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">data</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{data}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},c^{2}{\mathbf{I}})</annotation></semantics></math> be the data distribution.
Then the optimal consistency model <math id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> is given by</span></p>

<p id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For any <math id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> consider the following non-optimal consistency model</span></p>

<p id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Then, there exists an integer <math id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> for which increasing the number of sampling steps during multistep CM sampling beyond <math id="A3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> increases the Wasserstein-2 distance of the generated samples to the ground truth distribution.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">In this Gaussian setting, all intermediate noisy distributions <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p({\mathbf{x}}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p({\mathbf{x}}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=t\times{\mathbf{x}}_{1}+(1-t)\times{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p_{data},{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},{\mathbf{I}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=t\times{\mathbf{x}}_{1}+(1-t)\times{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p_{data},{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},{\mathbf{I}})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, remain Gaussian. As a result, the error of the non-optimal consistency model <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>ϵ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math> is:</span></p>

<p id="A3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text">and satisfies the error bound in <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 3.1 (Proof in Appendix). ‣ 3.1 Consistency Models are Flawed Multi-Step Generators ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> by choosing a small enough <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfies <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon^{2}&lt;\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon^{2}&lt;\delta</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Due to the Gaussian setting, both the optimal velocity from flow matching, <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{v}}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{v}}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the optimal denoiser, <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{D}}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{D}}^{*}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math>, have closed-form solutions.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">We first derive the denoiser. Following the framework of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, let <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p({\mathbf{x}};\sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p({\mathbf{x}};\sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the distribution obtained by adding independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> to the data. Then,</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
