<p id="A4.SS1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">Taking the limit as <math id="A4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\to t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\to t</annotation></semantics></math> gives:</p>
<table id="A4.E27" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A4.E27X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E27X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[\mathbf{F}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)\left(\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[\mathbf{F}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)\left(\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E27X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[\left\|\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[\left\|\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(27)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.5" class="ltx_p">which is exactly the standard flow matching loss.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Continuous-Time Consistency Models</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that the AYF-EMD objective introduced in <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 3.2 (Proof in Appendix). ‣ 3.2 Learning Flow Maps ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> also generalizes the continuous-time consistency model objective. Specifically, we prove that the AYF-EMD objective reduces to the continuous CM objective when <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=0</annotation></semantics></math>, up to a constant factor.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consider the AYF-EMD objective:</p>
<table id="A4.E28" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E28.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[w^{\prime}(t,s)\,\text{sign}(t-s)\,{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>sign</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[w^{\prime}(t,s)\,\text{sign}(t-s)\,{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(28)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Setting <math id="A4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=0</annotation></semantics></math> gives:</p>
<table id="A4.E29" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E29.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[w^{\prime}(t,0)\,{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,0)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,0)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t}\left[w^{\prime}(t,0)\,{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}^{\top}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,0)\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,0)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(29)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">since <math id="A4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sign}(t)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sign}(t)=1</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. Noting that <math id="A4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,0)</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the CM prediction at noise level <math id="A4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, this recovers the standard continuous-time CM objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Consistency Trajectory Models</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we discuss the connection to Consistency Trajectory Models (CTMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite>. Recall from the derivation of the AYF-EMD objective in <a href="#A3.SS2.SSS1" title="C.2.1 AYF-EMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2.1</span></a> that its gradient corresponds to the continuous-time limit of a discrete consistency loss. Interestingly, TCD uses this exact same discrete consistency loss to train its flow map, with a fixed discretization schedule. Therefore, the TCD objective can be seen as a discrete approximation of the AYF-EMD loss.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Flow Map Matching</h4>

<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we highlight the similarities and differences between our AYF objectives and the losses proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.1 </span>EMD</h5>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we will show the connection between our AYF-EMD objective and the EMD loss proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>. Recall the EMD loss from their work:</p>
<table id="A4.E30" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E30.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[w(t,s)\left\|\partial_{t}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)+\nabla_{{\mathbf{x}}}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)\cdot\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]=\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[w(t,s)\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]." <div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This loss can be derived in a similar fashion as our AYF-EMD loss by introducing a modification to <a href="#A3.E18" title="In Theorem C.2 (Restated from ). ‣ C.2.1 AYF-EMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>. Specifically, by replacing the second term <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t^{\prime}},t^{\prime},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t^{\prime}},t^{\prime},s)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t^{\prime}},t^{\prime},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t^{\prime}},t^{\prime},s)</annotation></semantics></math> and allowing gradients to flow through both terms, we recover the EMD loss from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Concretely, we can show that in the limit as <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the gradient of this objective with respect to <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> converges to:</p>

<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{\prime}(t,s)=w(t,s)\times|t-s|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{\prime}(t,s)=w(t,s)\times|t-s|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">which converges to the gradient of the EMD loss as <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that when deriving AYF-EMD, taking the limit of the discrete consistency loss when <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> only required dividing by <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, since the relevant term decays linearly in <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>. In contrast, the gradient in this case decays quadratically with respect to <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, which is why we divide by <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> before taking the limit.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The small difference in the AYF-EMD derivation, namely applying a stop-gradient operation on the second term in <a href="#A3.E18" title="In Theorem C.2 (Restated from ). ‣ C.2.1 AYF-EMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>, has a significant effect on training dynamics. Without it, one must backpropagate through the Jacobian-vector product (JVP) used to compute <math id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)}{\mathrm{d}t}</annotation></semantics></math>. This often introduces instability and slows down training.
However, with the stop-gradient operation, one must only compute the JVP without needing to backpropagate through it. Fortunately, modern autograd libraries like PyTorch support forward-mode automatic differentiation, which allows computing the JVP efficiently with minimal overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, applying the stop-gradient means the output of a large step with the flow map is pushed toward the output of following the PF-ODE trajectory for a bit and then doing a smaller step with the flow map. Without the stop-gradient, the small step is also encouraged to match the outcome of the large step, which is counterintuitive. This is because learning a flow map becomes more difficult as the interval length increases. Smaller steps are typically more reliable and offer better approximations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Ultimately, the decision to include or omit the stop-gradient operation in <a href="#A3.E18" title="In Theorem C.2 (Restated from ). ‣ C.2.1 AYF-EMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> leads to two fundamentally different derivations and objectives. In our experiments, only the AYF-EMD variant, where the stop-gradient is applied, was able to scale effectively to large-scale image datasets and produce high-quality outputs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">D.4.2 </span>LMD</h5>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An analogous connection can also be made between our AYF-LMD objective and the LMD loss from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>. Recall the LMD loss from their work:</p>
<table id="A4.E32" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E32.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[w(t,s)\left\|\partial_{s}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)-{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s),s)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em">∂</mo><mi>s</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[w(t,s)\left\|\partial_{s}{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)-{\mathbf{v}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s),s)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to before, we will show that by removing the stop-gradient operation from <a href="#A3.E21" title="In Theorem C.4 (Restated from ). ‣ C.2.2 AYF-LMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a> and allowing gradients to flow through both terms, we recover the LMD loss from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As before, applying the stop-gradient operation allows us to avoid backpropagating through the JVP, which speeds up training. Unlike the EMD case though, we found that the LMD loss from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al. [5]</a></cite> was already stable in practice and did not introduce training instabilities. Since both versions performed similarly in our experiments, we recommend using AYF-LMD for its improved training efficiency (note, however, that in all image generation experiments, we found AYF-EMD to perform better; see ablation study <a href="#A7.T5" title="In Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, the stop-gradient in this loss plays a similar role as in the other objective: we want the output of a large step of the flow map to match the result of taking a smaller step with the flow map, followed by integrating the PF-ODE.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Another way to understand this is through <a href="#A3.E21" title="In Theorem C.4 (Restated from ). ‣ C.2.2 AYF-LMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>. This loss fixes the smaller step <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> and optimizes the larger step <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> so that it aligns with the velocity field at the smaller step. As <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}\to s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}\to s</annotation></semantics></math>, we can think of <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> as fixed. The model then adjusts the slope of the flow map with respect to <math id="A4.SS4.SSS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> so that it matches the teacher flow at that point. Without the stop-gradient, the endpoint is no longer fixed and can also move to match the teacher, which changes the optimization behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.5 </span>MeanFlow Models</h4>

<div id="A4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we will show the connection to MeanFlow Models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, which are a concurrent work focused on training flow maps from scratch. We will show that the AYF-EMD objective reduces to the MeanFlow loss assuming an Euler parametrization of the flow map <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}+(s-t){\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}+(s-t){\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math>. This parametrization is inspired by the first-order DDIM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite> solver of diffusion models, which uses Euler Integration to solve the probability flow ODE.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recall the MeanFlow objective:</p>
<table id="A4.E34" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(34)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

</section>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Flow Maps in Prior and Concurrent Works</h3>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flow maps (or specific instances of them) have appeared in various prior works. In the previous section, we have derived relations to some prior and concurrent works already. In this section, we provide a broader overview. Broadly, prior works on flow maps can be grouped into discrete-time and continuous-time methods.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Discrete-time Flow Maps</h4>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flow maps were initially proposed as a natural generalization of consistency models (CMs), and early work primarily focused on discrete-time formulations built on discrete consistency losses.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consistency Trajectory Models (CTM)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> were the first to explicitly introduce and study flow maps. CTM trains discrete-time flow maps using a combination of discrete consistency loss, flow matching loss, and an adversarial loss. Notably, CTM was also the first to introduce <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>-sampling for stochastic sampling of flow maps. While the models produced high-quality samples, their performance depended heavily on the adversarial component, with a significant FID drop when it was removed.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectory Consistency Distillation</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite> builds on CTM, extending it to text-to-image generation. They empirically demonstrate that standard CMs degrade in quality as the number of function evaluations (NFEs) increases, a problem which is solved when using flow maps. These models can be viewed as a discrete variant of AYF, as shown in <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Consistency Trajectory Models ‣ Appendix D Connections to Existing Methods ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bidirectional CMs</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> observe that most prior work only trained flow maps in the denoising direction (<math id="A5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s&lt;t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s&lt;t</annotation></semantics></math>). They propose training on unordered timestep pairs, accelerating application like inversion, inpainting, interpolation, and blind restoration.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [37]</a></cite> trained CTMs connecting arbitrary distributions by operating within the flow matching framework instead of diffusions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In parallel, <span id="A5.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multistep CMs</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> attempted to address the poor multi-step behavior of standard CMs. They divide the denoising trajectory into subintervals and train separate CMs within each, achieving strong performance with as few as 2–8 steps. <span id="A5.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phased CMs</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>]</cite> adopt a similar idea but add adversarial training within each subinterval. These models effectively learn flow maps by training on <math id="A5.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> pairs where <math id="A5.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is the start of a fixed subinterval containing <math id="A5.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. This requires the inference step count to be pre-determined during training, and cannot be changed to trade off compute and quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Continuous-time Flow Maps</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">More recently, several methods have tackled training flow maps in continuous time.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flow Map Matching</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> provides a formal and rigorous analysis of continuous-time flow maps and proposes several continuous-time losses. However, their empirical validation is limited to small-scale experiments. In <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Consistency Trajectory Models ‣ Appendix D Connections to Existing Methods ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>, we discuss the connection between AYF and Flow Map Matching.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Shortcut Models</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> also operate in the continuous-time flow map setting. They propose an objective combining flow matching and a self-consistency loss. Their full loss (up to constants) is:</p>
<table id="A5.E36" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E36.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[\left\|{\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\left\|{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)-{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}\left({\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}\left({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,\frac{t+s}{2}\right),\frac{t+s}{2},s\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s}\left[\left\|{\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,t)-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\left\|{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)-{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}\left({\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}\left({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,\frac{t+s}{2}\right),\frac{t+s}{2},s\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(36)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where the flow map is parameterized as <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}+(s-t){\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}+(s-t){\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math>. Intuitively, the self-consistency term encourages agreement between one large step and two smaller intermediate steps along the PF-ODE denoising path. To train from scratch, they use the empirical estimate <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbf{x}}_{1}-{\mathbf{x}}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbf{x}}_{1}-{\mathbf{x}}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> in place of <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}</annotation></semantics></math>.Although their results on ImageNet-256 and CelebAHQ-256 are promising, they use suboptimal architectures and achieve significantly worse FID scores than state-of-the-art methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The Shortcut loss can also be used for distillation by replacing <math id="A5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}</annotation></semantics></math> with outputs from a pretrained velocity model. We include this variant in our ablations (see <a href="#A7.T5" title="In Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> for details).</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inductive Moment Matching</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">94</a>]</cite> is a recent method for training flow maps from scratch. It proposes using an MMD loss to align the <span id="A5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distributions</span> of <math id="A5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{r},r,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta^{-}}({\mathbf{x}}_{r},r,s)</annotation></semantics></math> over tuples <math id="A5.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,r,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,r,t)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying <math id="A5.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s&lt;r&lt;t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s&lt;r&lt;t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Concurrent Works</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Two concurrent works have also investigated training continuous-time flow maps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MeanFlow Models</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> study training flow maps from scratch using a loss closely related to our AYF-EMD objective. In fact, their formulation corresponds to a special case of AYF-EMD under an Euler flow map parameterization: <math id="A5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}+(s-t)\times{\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐟</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)={\mathbf{x}}_{t}+(s-t)\times{\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math>, as shown in <a href="#A4.SS5" title="D.5 MeanFlow Models ‣ Appendix D Connections to Existing Methods ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.5</span></a>. They refer to <math id="A5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{F}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> as the <span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Mean Flow</span> and use their objective to train flow maps from scratch, thereby being complementary to our work, which focuses on distillation. Their method achieves strong one- and two-step results on ImageNet 256x256, showing that the AYF-EMD objective is effective not just for distillation, but also for training from scratch.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">How to Build a Consistency Model</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> extends the authors’ prior work on Flow Map Matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, offering a deeper analysis of the EMD and LMD objectives. They also investigate the role of higher-order derivatives, finding them helpful in low-dimensional settings but largely ineffective in high-dimensional ones.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to these prior and concurrent works, AYF proposes new training objectives, leverages autoguidance for distillation, and shows how brief adversarial fine-tuning can boost performance without reducing diversity. Moreover, we provide new theoretical insights and for the first time analytically prove CMs’ deterioration with increased numbers of sampling steps. Finally, we overall scale flow map models to text-to-image generation and state-of-the-art few-step performance on ImageNet benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Experiment Details</h3>

<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>ImageNet Experiments</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For our ImageNet experiments, we use publicly available checkpoints from EDM2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. These models are first fine-tuned to align with the flow matching framework (see <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Training Tricks ‣ 3 Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a> for details) before being used as teacher models to distill a flow map. We run this finetuning stage for <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10,000</annotation></semantics></math> steps using a learning rate of <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.001</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.001</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the teacher model, we use checkpoints corresponding to the S and XS models, trained on 2147 million and 134 million images, respectively. During training, we randomize the guidance scale by sampling <math id="A6.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> uniformly from the range <math id="A6.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,3]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,3]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In all experiments, we apply tangent normalization and tangent warmup, following the approach introduced in sCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, setting <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=10000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=10000</annotation></semantics></math>. To ensure stable training, we define <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(t,s)=\frac{1}{|t-s|^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(t,s)=\frac{1}{|t-s|^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which removes the <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s-t)^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s-t)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> term—one arising from the proportional assumption (see <a href="#A3.SS2.SSS1" title="C.2.1 AYF-EMD ‣ C.2 Theorems: Flow Map Objectives ‣ Appendix C Proofs, Derivations and Theoretical Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2.1</span></a> for details) and another from the <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s-t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s-t)</annotation></semantics></math> coefficient of <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t,s)</annotation></semantics></math> in our flow map parameterization. We use a learning rate of <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and a batch size of 2048 for all experiments for a total of <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50,000</annotation></semantics></math> iterations. These experiments were performed using 32 NVIDIA A100 gpus and took approximately 24-48 hours to converge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A detailed algorithm can be seen in <a href="#alg1" title="In F.3 Training Algorithms ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Timestep scheduling</h6>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We sample the interval distance <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|t-s|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|t-s|</annotation></semantics></math> from a normal distribution <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>mean</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mtext>std</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by a sigmoid transformation. This prioritizes medium-length intervals and improves overall training stability. Once the interval length is determined, a random interval of that length is uniformly selected, with <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t&gt;s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t&gt;s</annotation></semantics></math> set as the two endpoints. Since we are only concerned with generation, we do not train on <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t&lt;s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t&lt;s)</annotation></semantics></math> pairs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We find <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}})=(-0.8,1.0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>mean</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>std</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}})=(-0.8,1.0)</annotation></semantics></math> works well for ImageNet-512, while <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}})=(-0.6,1.6)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>mean</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>std</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1.6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(P_{\text{mean}},P_{\text{std}})=(-0.6,1.6)</annotation></semantics></math> works well for ImageNet-64.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sampling hyperparameters</h6>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At inference time, we sweep the guidance scale <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> in the range <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,3]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,3]</annotation></semantics></math> and the sampling stochasticity <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> to determine optimal hyperparameters. <a href="#A6.T3" title="In Sampling hyperparameters ‣ F.1 ImageNet Experiments ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> summarizes the selected values. For <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-step sampling, intermediate timesteps <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are uniformly distributed over the interval <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.T3" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For completeness, we include the additional baselines from Table 2 of sCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> in <a href="#A6.T4" title="In Additional ImageNet512 baselines: ‣ F.1 ImageNet Experiments ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Our AYF models are able to outperform all methods using only 4 sampling steps.</p>

<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Adversarial Finetuning</h4>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For adversarial finetuning, we use the StyleGAN2 discriminator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> and follow the relativistic pairing GAN (RpGAN) formulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. The complete algorithm is provided in <a href="#alg2" title="In F.3 Training Algorithms ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The flow map is optimized by minimizing a combination of the AYF-EMD loss and a weighted RpGAN objective. To compute the adversarial loss, we perform one-step sampling with the flow map (i.e. setting <math id="A6.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t,s)=(1,0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t,s)=(1,0)</annotation></semantics></math>) to generate negative samples.
Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, we apply an adaptive weighting scheme to balance the AYF-EMD and adversarial terms. Additionally, we multiply the adversarial loss by a fixed coefficient <math id="A6.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> to ensure stable training. For the discriminator, we apply <math id="A6.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A6.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> regularization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> with a regularization weight of <math id="A6.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We use a learning rate of <math id="A6.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> for both networks and a batch size of 1024. Finetuning is run for approximately 3000 iterations using 32 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, taking around 4 hours in total.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Training Algorithms</h4>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide the full AYF algorithm in <a href="#alg1" title="In F.3 Training Algorithms ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, and the variant with adversarial finetuning in <a href="#alg2" title="In F.3 Training Algorithms ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>

<section id="A6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Text-to-Image Experiments</h4>

<div id="A6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For our text-to-image experiments, we distill FLUX.1-[dev] <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> into a few-step generator by fine-tuning a LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> on top of the FLUX base model. We use the AYF-EMD objective and train the LoRA for 10,000 iterations on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Each GPU fits a single <math id="A6.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\times 512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\times 512</annotation></semantics></math> image, resulting in a total batch size of 8. To manage memory, gradient checkpointing and gradient partitioning is used. We also warm up the tangent over the first 2000 iterations. Since FLUX.1-[dev] is guidance-distilled, we cannot use autoguidance and instead rely solely on the distilled guidance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We train our model using the text-to-image-2M dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> from Hugging Face, which contains over 2 million real and synthetic images. We filter this dataset and train only on the 100K images generated by FLUX.1-[dev] using text prompts from GPT-4o.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.5 </span>User Study Details</h4>

<div id="A6.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate our AYF-LoRA and compare it against TCD-LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>]</cite> and LCM-LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> (both based on SDXL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>), we conduct a user study with 47 participants.
We use a holdout set of 200 prompts generated by GPT-4o from the text-to-image-2M dataset. For each prompt, we generate five images using each of the three methods, all sampled with four steps from the same random seed, resulting in 1000 sets of three generated images.
Each participant is given a text prompt and one image from each method, with the image order randomized to prevent bias. Participants are asked to select the best image based on quality and text alignment or indicate a tie. <a href="#S5.F7" title="In 5 Experiments ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> summarizes the results. See <a href="#A6.F10" title="In F.5 User Study Details ‣ Appendix F Experiment Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> for a screenshot of the instruction.
The participants were paid 0.10$ per evaluation with an average evaluation time of 15-30s per decision, with an hourly average pay of 18$/hr.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.14603v1/figures/user_study_ui.jpg" id="A6.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/360;" width="381" height="360" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F10.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="A6.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Screenshot of instructions provided to the participants for the human evaluation study.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we isolate the effects of AYF’s core design choices and compare our method against recent baseline consistency model and flow map approaches (on ImageNet512). A summary of the results is provided in <a href="#A7.T5" title="In Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We begin by analyzing two key design decisions behind AYF: (1) using the AYF-EMD loss instead of AYF-LMD, and (2) applying autoguidance on the teacher model instead of classifier-free guidance (CFG), which is used by existing CM methods. To compare AYF-EMD and AYF-LMD, we first evaluate both qualitatively on a 2D toy dataset (<a href="#A7.F12" title="In Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>). In this setting, AYF-LMD significantly outperforms AYF-EMD. However, the trend reverses on image datasets, where AYF-EMD consistently yields better results. As shown in <a href="#A7.T5" title="In Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, AYF-EMD leads to significantly improved generation quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluate the impact of autoguidance. Replacing it with CFG consistently degrades performance across all sampling steps, highlighting the benefit of autoguidance during distillation. This difference can also be visually seen in the 2D setting (<a href="#A7.F12" title="In Appendix G Ablation Studies ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we compare AYF against baseline methods. Against <span id="A7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">sCD</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, the current state-of-the-art consistency model, we observe that increasing the number of steps consistently degrades performance beyond 4 steps. In contrast, AYF’s performance stabilizes after 8 steps and remains consistently better at 4 steps, narrowing the gap between the few-step student and the multi-step teacher. AYF achieves this improved multi-step performance by having slightly worse single-step generations. This is expected considering that both models share the same parameter budget but AYF solves a more difficult task. However, performing a short adversarial finetuning on top of a pretrained AYF model significantly boosts performance across all sampling steps (see <a href="#A2.F8" title="In Appendix B Limitations ‣ Appendix ‣ Align Your Flow:Scaling Continuous-Time Flow Map Distillation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>), overcoming this limitation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Note that also with autoguidance replaced by CFG, we still outperform sCD for all steps except for single-step generation. This trend remains when re-training sCD with an autoguided teacher and comparing with the full AYF with autoguided teacher. These analyses show that while autoguidance boosts performance, our model is superior to the previous state-of-the-art CM for all sampling step settings except single-step generation also when comparing under the same guidance scheme. This is due to our novel objectives for state-of-the-art continuous-time flow map training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to <span id="A7.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Shortcut models</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, which we re-implemented, AYF again outperforms them consistently. While Shortcut models improve steadily with increasing NFEs, their few-step performance is significantly worse than both AYF and sCD. Unlike shortcut models, AYF reaches strong performance earlier and plateaus around 8 steps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.F12" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F12.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="A7.F12.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Four-step samples from distilled AYF flow maps trained using the AYF-EMD and AYF-LMD objectives for a 2D distribution.</span></figcaption>
